report:
### Conclusion
The health claim is **true** and backed by robust clinical evidence. Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials demonstrate that adjunctive (add-on) cannabidiol (CBD) significantly reduces convulsive seizure frequency in children and young adults with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome.

### Supporting Evidence
1. **Pivotal Clinical Trial:** A randomized controlled trial published in *The New England Journal of Medicine* evaluated 120 children and young adults with Dravet syndrome. Add-on cannabidiol resulted in a significantly greater reduction in monthly convulsive seizure frequency compared to placebo over a 14-week treatment period (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618).
2. **Dose-Ranging Studies:** A 199-patient trial published in *JAMA Neurology* confirmed that adjunctive cannabidiol at daily doses of both 10 mg/kg and 20 mg/kg was superior to placebo in reducing convulsive seizure frequency (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458).
3. **Systematic Reviews:** Evidence syntheses confirm that add-on CBD provides clinically meaningful reductions in convulsive seizures in Dravet syndrome, though it is accompanied by adverse events such as somnolence, decreased appetite, diarrhea, and elevated liver enzymes (https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s40263-020-00708-6.pdf).
4. **Regulatory Approval:** Based on these clinical trials, the U.S. FDA approved Epidiolex (a prescription cannabidiol oral solution) specifically for treating seizures associated with Dravet syndrome (https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-drug-comprised-active-ingredient-derived-marijuana-treat-rare-severe-forms).
